prompt:
An industrial on-site power generation facility uses fuel to generate electrical power through a three-stage conversion process:
[FIGURE PLACEHOLDER: Block diagram showing three sequential stages of a thermal power plant. Stage 1: Boiler (efficiency eta_1 = 82%). Stage 2: Steam turbine (efficiency eta_2 = 40%). Stage 3: Electrical generator (efficiency eta_3 = 95%). Wasted heat pathways exit from each stage into the environment.]
- Stage 1 (Boiler): converts chemical energy of fuel into thermal energy of steam with an efficiency of 82% (0.82).
- Stage 2 (Steam turbine): converts thermal energy of steam into rotational kinetic energy of a shaft with an efficiency of 40% (0.40).
- Stage 3 (Electrical generator): converts shaft kinetic energy into electrical energy with an efficiency of 95% (0.95).
(a) (i) Explain why the overall efficiency of this three-stage system is found by multiplying the stage efficiencies rather than averaging them. [1]
(ii) Calculate the overall efficiency of the power generation facility. [2]
(b) Chemical energy is supplied to the boiler at an input rate of 2.5 MW.
(i) Calculate the electrical power output delivered by the generator. [1]
(ii) Calculate the total rate of energy dissipation across the entire system. [1]
(iii) Identify which stage dissipates energy at the highest rate, and name the primary form of this dissipated energy. [1]

parts.description: Calculate overall system efficiency from stage efficiencies
Calculate electrical power output from input rate
Calculate total system rate of energy dissipation
Identify stage with greatest dissipation and form of energy

part_enrichment.guidance: Award B1 for explaining that each subsequent stage operates only on the useful output of the previous stage.
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Vaguely saying 'because each stage has losses' without explaining compounding.
Adding percentages together or computing an average.

part_enrichment.guidance: Award A1 for P_out = 0.3116 * 2.5 MW = 0.78 MW (or 780 kW).
Award A1 for 2.5 - 0.779 = 1.72 MW (accept 1.7 MW or 1.72 * 10^6 W).
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Calculating wasted power for only one stage.

part_enrichment.guidance: Award B1 for Stage 2 (turbine) AND thermal energy (heat in steam / cooling water).
part_enrichment.common_pitfalls: Guessing the boiler without checking the 60% loss in the turbine.

answer:
(a)(i) Each successive stage receives only the useful energy output delivered by the preceding stage, so the useful fractions compound multiplicatively.
(a)(ii) 31% (or 31.2% / 0.31)
(b)(i) 0.78 MW (or 780 kW / 7.8 * 10^5 W)
(b)(ii) 1.7 MW (or 1.72 MW / 1.72 * 10^6 W)
(b)(iii) Stage 2 (the turbine); internal thermal energy (heat in exhaust steam / cooling water).

mark_scheme.criterion: (a)(i) explains that each stage acts on the reduced output of the preceding stage (losses compound)
(b)(ii) 1.7 MW or 1.72 MW (P_dissipated = 2.5 MW - 0.779 MW = 1.721 MW)

hints: In (a)(i), think about what enters each subsequent stage.
In (a)(ii), multiply the three fractional efficiencies.
In (b)(i), multiply total input power (2.5 MW) by overall efficiency.
In (b)(ii), subtract electrical output power from total input power.
In (b)(iii), compare the percentage wasted at each stage (boiler wastes 18%, turbine wastes 60%, generator wastes 5%).
solution:
(a)(i) The overall efficiency is the product of stage efficiencies because each successive stage receives only the useful energy delivered by the preceding stage. The useful energy output of stage 1 becomes the total energy input to stage 2, compounding the fractional transfers.
(a)(ii) eta_overall = eta_1 * eta_2 * eta_3 = 0.82 * 0.40 * 0.95 = 0.3116 = 31% (or 31.2%).
(b)(i) P_electrical = eta_overall * P_fuel = 0.3116 * 2.5 MW = 0.779 MW approx 0.78 MW (780 kW).
(b)(ii) Total rate of dissipation = P_in - P_out = 2.5 MW - 0.779 MW = 1.721 MW approx 1.7 MW (1.72 * 10^6 W).
(b)(iii) Stage 2 (the turbine) dissipates the most energy: it wastes 60% of the steam energy delivered to it (0.60 * (0.82 * 2.5 MW) = 1.23 MW). The primary form of this dissipated energy is internal thermal energy (heat transferred to cooling water/condenser).
teacher_walkthrough: Comprehensive multipart problem on multi-stage thermodynamic efficiency.
Reinforces that thermal power stations are primarily constrained by turbine thermodynamic efficiency.
Check that all 6 marks align with the response structure and mark scheme.

provenance.abstract_pattern: multi-stage thermal power plant efficiency audit and waste analysis
provenance.independence_statement: Authored as an original multipart question analyzing a three-stage power station efficiency and thermal loss chain.
